What this app does, and where it stops

Android 13 lets the system keep a separate language for each app. Settings → Apps → App language only lists apps that ship a locale config, so most apps never appear there even though the underlying override works for them too.
This app writes that same per-app override directly, for any installed package. Your phone can stay in Japanese while one app runs in English and another in 简体中文.
It only changes the language an app is told to use. If the app does not ship resources for that language, Android falls back to the app’s default and nothing visible changes.
Search by app name or package name. Use the menu to include system apps.
Pick a preset or type any BCP 47 tag, such as pt-BR or zh-Hant-TW.
Apply writes the locale; a running app may not notice until it restarts. Apply & Restart force-stops the app and reopens it, which is what makes the change visible in most apps.
Choosing System Default removes the override and hands the app back to the phone’s language. Apps with an override are marked with a dot and can be listed on their own with the Configured filter.
Per-app locales did not exist before Android 13, and cannot be emulated on Android 12.

Where the language lives in an in-app setting or in your account on their server, the app ignores the system locale entirely. Several Chinese super-apps work this way.
Screens rendered from the server, and much of what appears in a WebView, follow the account or the browser’s Accept-Language header instead.
Some OEM builds reject it. The locale is still written — close the app from Recents yourself. The app says so when this happens.
One user profile at a time.
Changes apply to the user this app is installed in; a work profile has its own copy of everything.
Shizuku must be restarted after every reboot.
Until it is, the list still shows what is configured but nothing can be changed.

Everything happens on the device. The app has no internet permission and sends nothing anywhere. Its core feature needs the complete installed-app list, including package names, labels, icons, current locale settings, and officially declared languages, so you can select any app. Your choices stay local, and the system remains the source of truth for locales.
Four steps, no root, no computer required

Writing another app’s locale requires system permissions that are reserved for the platform, so no ordinary app can hold them. Shizuku runs a small service as the shell user — the same user behind adb — and lets this app route that one call through it. Nothing here needs root, and the app gains no permission of its own.
From Google Play, F-Droid, or the GitHub releases page. On a rooted device you can install Sui instead — it starts by itself and survives reboots.

Enable Developer options → Wireless debugging, keep that screen open, then open Shizuku and tap “Start via Wireless debugging”. The first time, Shizuku asks you to pair using the pairing code shown under Wireless debugging.
…or start it from a computer instead

Come back here and accept the Shizuku prompt. The status at the top of this screen says Connected as soon as everything is in place.

The service is not a background app; it dies when the device restarts, and the app list here goes back to being read-only until you repeat step 2 or 3. Sui, on a rooted device, is the only way around that.
